column4: The section says the root رءي includes doing something so people see; this ayah stages that exact motive in spending and says such alms are nullified by reminders and harm.
It directly names spending wealth رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ, the scene the section sets beside 90:6–7: public expenditure meant to establish the spender's reputation.
The section develops showing an act so people see it; this uses يُرَاءُونَ for the same public performance, here in prayer rather than spending.
The section contrasts a spender's boastful tally with the destination of wealth; this man gathers مال and عدّده, making accumulation and counting his practice.
The source section names ح س ب as both counting status and supposition; here يَحْسَبُ that his مال will make him everlasting turns the same false reckoning toward wealth's promised permanence.
The section's ه ل ك gloss includes something ceasing to exist; the garden owner says he does not think this garden will تَبِيدَ, a direct denial that his property can perish.
The section notes حُسْبَانًا as a dictionary sense for fire sent from the sky; the companion names that very sky-blast as the reversal of the owner's confidence that his garden cannot perish.
The ruined owner turns his hands over مَا أَنفَقَ فِيهَا; unlike 90:6's proud total, the expenditure is now remembered as a loss after the garden and its fruit are destroyed.
The source section pairs its boast أَهْلَكْتُ مَالًا with later loss; this speaker confesses مَالِيَهْ brought him no benefit when his worldly account is tested.
The section explains ه ل ك as disappearance and failure; this speaker says هَلَكَ عَنِّي سُلْطَانِيَهْ, extending the loss from wealth to the power he thought he had.

Qarun claims his treasure was given because of knowledge عِندِي, then the verse says God had أَهْلَكَ earlier generations; his self-credit meets the section's root ه ل ك and reverses boastful possession.
The section's رءي discussion links seeing to public self-display; this opens the paired warning that a person can overstep when he treats himself as self-sufficient.
The source section distinguishes being seen from seeing oneself; this says رَآهُ اسْتَغْنَى, locating arrogance in the person's own view of his sufficiency.
The section contrasts a counted expenditure with what wealth is for; here the hoarded gold and silver are returned as punishment, and their owners are told to taste what they كنزوا.
The section opposes public praise to counting a gift as reward with God; these feeders say they seek only وجه الله and no recompense or thanks from people.
The section's boast is about having consumed wealth; this person يُؤْتِي مَالَهُ seeking purification, so the same material act is defined by its purpose.
Where the section's speaker seeks a name among people, this giver acts only ابتغاء وجه ربه الأعلى, making the audience of the deed the decisive difference.
This directly sets a boundary on the section's boast: after spending, believers do not follow what they أَنفَقُوا with مَنًّا or harm.

The section's ل س ن and ش ف ه dictionary glosses concern praise on people's tongues; Abraham asks God to grant him لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ, so lasting mention is sought as a gift from God rather than manufactured by a boast.
The garden owner says أَنَا أَكْثَرُ مِنكَ مَالًا وَأَعَزُّ نَفَرًا, an explicit boast of wealth and standing that closely parallels the section's self-advertised expenditure.
The same owner assumes that even if returned to his Lord he will receive a better outcome; the verse extends his wealth-based confidence from this life into the account beyond it.
His companion says he should have acknowledged مَا شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ; this names the dependence missing from the owner's self-attributed wealth and abundance.
After the sky-blast named in 18:40, the companion adds that the garden's water may sink; this completes the section's contrast between imagined permanence and property disappearing.
After the garden is lost, no فِئَة can help its owner; the scene shows that wealth and social standing cannot supply the protection he presumed.
The Qur'an follows the garden story with a parable of worldly life as rain-grown plants that dry and scatter; it makes the owner's loss an instance of how possessions pass.
This states the section's unspoken measure: المال والبنون are worldly adornment, while enduring good deeds are better with God than a large worldly total.
The section's speaker assumes no one saw him; this book of deeds leaves nothing small or great uncounted, directly reversing that assumption with an exact account.
Qarun is introduced with treasures whose keys burden a group of strong men; the verse makes possession itself the spectacle behind his claim in 28:78.
Moses tells Qarun to seek the Hereafter with what God gave him, do good, and not فساد in the land; this gives a direct use and limit for the wealth Qarun treats as self-made status.
Qarun comes out in his adornment and people wish for his position; this stages the public gaze and reputation that the section says the spender wants his claim to produce.
Those given knowledge say God's reward is better for one who believes and acts rightly; their measure counters the crowd's admiration of Qarun's display.
The earth swallows Qarun and his house; this is a concrete instance of the section's ه ل ك theme, wealth and its owner vanishing together.
The onlookers reverse their wish for Qarun's position once they see his fate, exposing how unreliable public admiration is as a measure of wealth.

This distinguishes visible charity from concealed giving and says the latter is better for the poor; it directly tests the section's tension between wanting one's expenditure seen and giving for its recipient.
The verse names spending by night and day, secretly and openly, with reward from the Lord; it makes visibility optional where the section's boaster makes being seen the point.
The section names احتسبت بكذا أجرا عند الله as counting an act for reward with God; this says spending is for one's own good while seeking God's face, not people's acclaim.
This adjacent charity teaching says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm; speech can serve the needy without turning a gift into a public claim.
These people feed the needy, orphan, and captive; the section's final contrast is between spending to be praised and actual provision reaching vulnerable people.
The source section names ح س ب for counting reward with God; this giver has no favor owed to anyone to repay, clarifying that the gift is not a social debt or reputation purchase.
The command gives relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due; it directs wealth toward recipients, answering the section's criticism that the boast counts amount but not destination.
Calling wasteful spenders brothers of Satan draws a boundary around treating depletion itself as virtue, as the boastful speaker does when he says he consumed much.
The image of a hand chained to the neck or stretched all the way out rejects both hoarding and unmeasured depletion; it gives a measure for the section's bare quantity-count.
The believers' spending is neither extravagant nor miserly but balanced; this directly replaces the section's boast in sheer amount with a measure of how wealth is used.
Righteousness includes giving beloved wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, and those who ask; it makes recipients and motive, not the spender's public total, the measure.
Asked what to spend, the answer names parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers; it supplies the destination the section says the boaster's accounting omits.
The verse ties righteousness to spending from what one loves; it makes the cost and moral purpose of giving matter more than advertising a large amount already consumed.
The section's قول dictionary branch includes a reputation spreading among people; this condemns those who love to be praised بِمَا لَمْ يَفْعَلُوا, isolating the fame-seeking that animates the boast.
The command warns against leaving home بَطَرًا وَرِئَاءَ النَّاسِ; it repeats the section's root رءي in a scene of arrogant public display.

This condemns those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way; 9:35 then turns that hoarded wealth into punishment, the boundary opposite treating a large expenditure as an achievement.
Some promise that if God gives them wealth they will give charity; this is a spoken claim like the section's, but the next verses test whether the words govern their use of wealth.
After receiving God's bounty, they become miserly; this exposes the promise in 9:75 as words that do not govern the use of wealth.
The passage says God knows their secret and private talk; this adds divine knowledge to the broken public promise and counters the thought that conduct escapes notice.

The section links speech and fame to how people talk about a person; this verse shows people criticizing both wealthy and poor voluntary contributors, making public judgment part of the spending scene.
The righteous have in their wealth a known right for the asker and deprived; this turns the section's image of requests exhausting a holder into an assigned claim of the needy.
This says a known right exists in the believers' wealth, then names the asker and deprived in 70:25; this ayah establishes that giving is an obligation, not a boastful surplus count.
The neighboring ayah specifies that the known right is for السائل والمحروم; it identifies the recipients whom the section says the spender's tally leaves unnamed.
A person interprets abundant provision as أَكْرَمَنِ, making wealth a public measure of personal honor just as the section exposes a boastful material tally.
The paired claim that restricted provision means أَهَانَنِ shows the same false equation in reverse: amount of wealth is not a reliable measure of honor.
The rebuke says they do not honor the orphan; it turns the claimed honor of abundance toward the actual treatment of a vulnerable person.
They do not urge feeding the poor; this names the omission that the section sets against real spending on the orphan and needy.
They consume inheritance greedily, shifting the focus from a wealth total to how it is acquired and used.
The passage says they love wealth intensely; this names the attachment underneath boastful claims of having spent or possessed much.
The surah begins by linking denial of judgment to conduct toward the orphan and poor, the moral contrast the section makes between public display and useful giving.
This person repels the orphan, opposite the section's final image of spending to feed and care for the vulnerable.
He does not urge feeding the poor; this directly reverses the section's feeding scene and makes withholding, not a boastful total, the moral evidence.
The next warning turns to prayer performed carelessly; it carries the passage's critique from withholding help toward public religious performance.
Their prayer is heedless, completing the context for the showy prayer in 107:6; the section's public-spending scene likewise asks what an act is for.
The punished ask what brought them to Saqar; the following answers connect the outcome to neglect of worship and the poor, giving an afterlife account of the opposite conduct.
They answer that they were not among those who prayed; this is one part of the answer sequence, whose next ayah specifies failure to feed the poor.
They say وَلَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ; the afterlife account judges the actual absence of feeding, the act the section says a mere spending boast cannot replace.
The garden owners swear to harvest its fruit in the morning, introducing another wealth scene whose outcome depends on whether provision is shared.
Their plan makes no allowance for the poor; it reveals before the loss that the garden's abundance is being counted as private property.
A calamity from their Lord passes over the garden while they sleep, making the expected harvest vanish without their control.
By morning the garden is like a harvested field, a concrete image of wealth gone that answers the boast of having consumed much.
The owners call one another early to carry out the plan; this continues the scene of confidently managing a harvest that has already been lost.
They go to the crop intending to harvest it, preserving their expectation before they see what happened.
They say not to let any poor person enter the garden; this makes the withheld destination of their property explicit.
When they see the garden, they say they must have lost their way; the expected property is gone, rather than available to support their status.
They recognize they were deprived, naming the reversal from planned abundance to loss.
The most moderate among them asks why they did not glorify God; this identifies the omitted acknowledgment of the source of provision.
They say سُبْحَانَ رَبِّنَا and confess they were wrongdoers; their speech after loss contrasts with the section's self-crediting boast before loss.
They admit they were transgressors, naming the wrong in their handling of the garden rather than celebrating its quantity.
They hope their Lord will replace it with something better; after loss, their hope is directed to God rather than to property as self-sufficient status.
The parable is followed by a warning that the punishment of the Hereafter is greater; this completes the scene's movement from worldly loss to account.
Spending in God's way is pictured as a grain multiplying into many ears; unlike the section's depleted tally, this expenditure is not simply gone but grows by God's measure.
Those who spend seeking God's pleasure are likened to a garden that yields fruit; it makes the purpose of expenditure, not its publicity, determine its result.
A garden with palms, vines, and offspring is struck by a fiery whirlwind in old age; this specific destruction of a valued holding parallels the section's loss-of-wealth scenes.
The command is to spend good things earned, not choose inferior goods for giving; this qualifies the section's point that a large amount alone says nothing about its destination or quality.
The section names ح س ب as supposition and as counting reward; this says God knows whatever is spent or vowed, putting both public and hidden acts within divine knowledge.
The section's ش ف ه dictionary branch pictures requests so numerous that a holder is exhausted; this verse presents needy people who do not ask persistently, so need may remain unseen by the crowd.
What disbelievers spend is likened to a freezing wind striking a crop of people who wronged themselves; the image makes expenditure that fails to yield good a concrete loss.
Wealth and children are called a trial, giving the section's possessions a moral test rather than treating their quantity as proof of honor.
The parable introduces two men and gives one of them two gardens; this establishes the wealth-and-audience scene developed in the following verses.
Both gardens yield their produce and a river runs between them; this shows the abundance supporting the boast in 18:34.
The companion reminds him that God created him from dust and a drop; this answers the owner's self-sufficiency with his dependence as a created person.
The companion states that God is his Lord and that he associates no one with Him; this answers the garden owner's false confidence with a different account of power.
After the owner's loss, protection belongs to God the True; this completes the garden scene's reversal of wealth as a source of lasting security.
The section's ل س ن dictionary gloss is praise on people's tongues; this says God granted Abraham's family لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ, making good remembrance a divine gift.
The command not to turn one's cheek in contempt or walk proudly sets a boundary on the self-display that the section locates in a wealth boast.
Two receivers sit on the right and left as the person speaks; this begins the context that answers the section's question whether anyone saw the speaker.
The section's قول root is the man's spoken boast; this says no word is uttered without a ready watcher, directly answering the assumption that no one saw.
The verse says not to claim yourselves pure because God knows who is mindful; it counters the section's attempt to secure a reputation through self-report.
Worldly life, wealth, and growth are likened to rain-fed plants that yellow and scatter; this gives a broad image of possessions passing rather than lasting.
The verse says not to grieve what passes or exult in what is given, and condemns boastful pride; it directly corrects the emotional accounting behind the section's boast.
The warning not to let wealth and children distract from God's remembrance identifies possessions as a competing allegiance rather than a source of security.
A dying person wishes for more time to give charity; this reverses the section's past-tense boast with regret that giving was postponed until the account is near.
Wealth and children are a trial, while great reward is with God; this reframes the section's material total as something by which a person is tested.
The person given his book in his left hand begins his lament; this sets the judgment scene in which he says his wealth did not help him in 69:28.
He wishes he had not been given his record, continuing the account context that turns a worldly boast into helpless regret.
He wishes death had ended everything, intensifying the regret before his explicit admission about wealth and power.
The passage identifies disbelief in God as part of the punished person's conduct; the following ayah adds that he did not urge feeding the poor.
He did not urge feeding the poor; this is the concrete failure adjacent to the lost wealth and power of 69:28–29.
The feeders fulfill vows and fear a difficult day; it supplies the judgment-facing motive developed by their feeding and refusal of human reward.
They say they fear a frowning, distressful day; this completes the motive for the feeding in 76:8–9 and contrasts with a spender seeking earthly praise.
The protected person is described immediately before the one who gives his wealth in 92:18; the sequence connects avoiding the Fire with purposeful expenditure.
The giver will be satisfied; this completes the passage's contrast between public acclaim and the final outcome sought from God.
The warning about seeing oneself as self-sufficient is followed by the return to the Lord; this gives the section's false self-assessment an account beyond worldly appearance.
The section's رءي discussion concerns being seen and acting for an audience; this asks whether the person knows that God sees, answering 90:7 directly.
Every atom-weight of good is seen; this overturns the section's speaker's assumption that his act escaped notice and that only his claimed total matters.
Every atom-weight of evil is seen as well; together with 99:7 it makes the unseen account include what the boast leaves out.
Rivalry in increasing worldly advantage distracts people; this is a close parallel to using a count of wealth and social standing as a public boast.
The rivalry lasts until people reach the graves; it carries the section's contrast between passing worldly totals and the account beyond them.
People will be asked about نعيم; this makes worldly provision answerable, unlike the boast that records only how much was spent.
The hoarder and counter is warned that he will be cast into the Crusher; this gives the counting scene introduced in 104:2–3 its consequence.
The Crusher is described as Allah's kindled fire; the punishment follows the wealth-hoarding and false security named just before it.
The verse says these people come to prayer lazily and spend only reluctantly; it makes expenditure itself a test of sincerity, beyond the section's boast of having spent much.
Some Bedouins treat what they spend as a loss or penalty and await misfortune for the believers; this is a direct contrary account of spending to the section's boastful claim.
Other Bedouins treat their spending as a means of closeness to God and the Messenger; the verse gives the opposite purpose from counting expenditure for public reputation.

The verse distinguishes wealth given to increase among people's possessions from charity given seeking God's face, which is multiplied; this directly separates public advantage from divine accounting.
These believers spend from what God provided secretly and openly, seeking a trade that will not fail; it answers the section's depleted tally with expenditure whose return is secured with God.
The next ayah says God will give them their full reward and increase them from His bounty; it completes 35:29's image of a trade that does not perish.
The source section's lisan and shafah dictionary glosses concern praise among people; this says honor belongs to God, and that good words and righteous deeds rise to Him.

The people say they did not hide themselves expecting their hearing, sight, and skins to testify against them, but thought God did not know much of their deeds; this directly reverses the section's assumption that no one saw.
This person withholds and considers himself self-sufficient, a close parallel to the section's false self-assessment and a reversal of its boast about consuming wealth.
He also denies the best; the verse identifies the belief that accompanies his withholding, rather than treating his wealth as an achievement.
God eases him toward hardship; this continues the reversal of the self-sufficient person's estimate of what his wealth secures.
When he falls, his wealth does not benefit him; this directly counters the section's speaker treating the use or loss of money as a boast.
The command not to oppress the orphan reverses the treatment of vulnerable people against which the section sets its giving.
The command not to repel the asker connects to the section's ش ف ه dictionary sense of requests exhausting a holder, but directs the holder to respond without rejection.
The section's قول and lisan discussion concerns public mention; this commands the hearer to speak of the Lord's favor, making remembrance of the giver the ground of speech rather than self-praise.
The hypocrites show their prayer to people and remember God little; this is another Qur'anic formulation of the section's root رءي as public performance.
The day comes when mouths are sealed and hands speak while feet testify; the speaker's own body answers the section's boastful spoken claim and assumption of no witness.
The verse says that if people possessed the treasuries of their Lord's mercy they would still withhold for fear of spending; this names the opposite calculation to a boast about consuming wealth.
People are called to spend in God's way, and the verse says some are miserly and that the one who withholds only withholds from himself; this reverses the section's boastful accounting of wealth.
Believers are told to spend from what God has made them successors over; the verse makes possession entrusted by God, against the speaker's self-crediting total.
The Ansar prefer others over themselves even when in need; this gives a concrete form of giving whose motive is another person's benefit, not applause.
The command says to spend for your own good and praises those protected from their own stinginess; this directly contrasts giving with hoarding or self-serving display.
The surah opens with a warning to those who give short measure; it brings the section's concern with counting wealth into a concrete scene of dishonest measurement.
They take full measure when measuring for themselves; this exposes the self-favoring calculation behind treating one's own total as the only relevant account.
They give others less when measuring or weighing for them; this reverses the speaker's self-presentation by judging the amount from the recipient's side.
Those who withhold what God has given are warned that it will be placed around their necks; this counters treating retained wealth as a safe measure of one's standing.

The verse lists accumulated gold and silver, horses, livestock, and crops among worldly attractions; it supplies concrete forms of wealth behind the section's account of مال and its older livestock sense.
The source section's dictionary gloss says Arab wealth was often livestock; this verse names cattle among the provisions given to a people, showing that material wealth could be herds.
The question asks whether wealth and children are thought to be good things hastened to people; it exposes the false measure of favor that the section's self-assessing spender assumes.
The next ayah answers that such people do not perceive; it completes the correction of the assumption in 23:55 that abundant possessions prove success.
The command to give full measure and weigh with a straight balance offers a concrete standard against self-serving calculation of amounts.
Believers are told to spend from what God provided before a Day with no trade or friendship; this places expenditure within an account that public reputation cannot settle.
Satan's promise of poverty gives a specific fear behind withholding wealth; it contrasts with the section's claim that a large expenditure is only a lost sum.
These people are not distracted by trade from God's remembrance, prayer, and giving; this counters making wealth and public notice the center of one's conduct.
The command joins fair measure and balance with guarding an orphan's property; it connects the section's account of quantities to the vulnerable person whose due can be lost.
The verse warns not to be impressed by the hypocrites' wealth and children; it addresses the audience response that a public material display seeks.
This repeats the warning not to be impressed by their wealth and children; its recurrence underlines that visible abundance is not evidence of divine favor.
This follows the catalogue of worldly attractions in 3:14 with what is better with God; it supplies the measure beyond the wealth and livestock just listed.

The source section uses لُبَدًا for wealth in heaps; this ayah uses a related form for a crowd pressing around the servant. The sense differs, so this is a weak possible echo: abundance and a public audience meet in the section, though the crowd here belongs to a different scene.
